```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 5.5)
```

```{r setup}
library(osmnxr)
g <- ox_example("olinda")
```

Routing in `osmnxr` runs in the Rust core (Dijkstra, Yen, multi-source). We use
the bundled real network of central Olinda, Brazil, so this runs offline.

## Shortest path by distance

Snap two coordinates to the nearest nodes, then route between them:

```{r}
orig <- ox_nearest_nodes(g, x = -34.8553, y = -8.0089)
dest <- ox_nearest_nodes(g, x = -34.8505, y = -8.0125)
route <- ox_route_shortest(g, orig, dest, weight = "length")
route
```

The result is an `sf` tibble: the route's cost, the node `osmid`s traversed
and its merged street geometry, ready to map. (`ox_shortest_path()` returns
just the vector of node ids, when that is all you need.)

```{r}
plot(g, col = "grey80", lwd = 0.6)
plot(sf::st_geometry(route), col = "#b7410e", lwd = 3, add = TRUE)
route_xy <- sf::st_coordinates(g$nodes)[match(route$path[[1]], g$nodes$osmid), ]
points(route_xy[c(1, nrow(route_xy)), ], pch = 19, col = "#0d3b66", cex = 1.2)
```

## Travel time instead of distance

Real routing usually minimises *time*, not distance. Impute free-flow speeds
from each road's class, derive per-edge travel times, then route on them
(Boeing 2025, `routing` module):

```{r}
g <- ox_add_edge_travel_times(g)
head(g$edges[c("highway", "length", "speed_kph", "travel_time")])

route_t <- ox_shortest_path(g, orig, dest, weight = "travel_time")
# may differ: the fastest route is not always the shortest
identical(route_t, route$path[[1]])
```

## Route alternatives

`ox_route_shortest(k = ...)` returns the *k* shortest loopless routes (Yen's
algorithm) — useful for comparing options or modelling redundancy:

```{r}
ox_route_shortest(g, orig, dest, k = 3, weight = "travel_time")
```

## Routing with road preferences

Often the best route is not simply the fastest one: a dispatcher may want to
keep trucks off residential streets, a cyclist may want to stay on them.
`ox_add_edge_penalties()` turns that preference into a per-edge column — here,
the metres each edge spends on calm residential road classes:

```{r}
g <- ox_add_edge_penalties(g, c(residential = 1, living_street = 1))
head(g$edges[c("highway", "length", "penalty")])
```

The *soft* version just folds the penalty into the routing weight (an ordinary
shortest path that trades seconds against residential metres at a fixed rate).
The interesting questions, though, are *hard*: what is the fastest route using
**at most** some budget of residential metres, and what does the whole
trade-off curve look like? `ox_route_pareto()` answers the second — it
enumerates every Pareto-optimal route exactly (bicriteria label-setting in the
Rust core; one-way streets respected):

```{r}
o2 <- ox_nearest_nodes(g, x = -34.85445, y = -8.01503)
d2 <- ox_nearest_nodes(g, x = -34.84853, y = -8.00431)
front <- ox_route_pareto(g, o2, d2, weight = "travel_time", resource = "penalty")
front[c("cost", "resource")]
```

Each successive route is a little slower and a little calmer; no other route
beats any of them on both criteria. Plotted, the alternatives fan out between
the fast arterial option and the quiet residential one:

```{r}
plot(g, col = "grey85", lwd = 0.6)
cols <- grDevices::hcl.colors(nrow(front), "Zissou 1")
plot(sf::st_geometry(front), add = TRUE, col = cols, lwd = 2.5)
```

`ox_route_constrained()` answers the first question — the exact constrained
shortest path for one chosen budget:

```{r}
best <- ox_route_constrained(g, o2, d2, weight = "travel_time",
                             resource = "penalty",
                             budget = stats::median(front$resource))
best[c("cost", "resource")]
```

On metro-sized networks where enumerating the exact front gets expensive,
`ox_route_constrained(..., method = "lagrangian")` solves the same problem by
Lagrangian relaxation — a handful of plain Dijkstra runs — returning a
feasible route together with a proven lower bound on the optimal cost (a
message reports the duality gap whenever optimality is not certified).

(For a road that is temporarily closed, don't penalize it — mask it: drop the
edge, or set its weight to `Inf`, before routing.)

## Isochrones (service areas)

An isochrone is the area reachable from an origin within a budget. With
`travel_time` as the weight, cutoffs are in seconds — here, 1- and 2-minute
drive-time service areas from a central point:

```{r}
centre <- ox_nearest_nodes(g, x = -34.8553, y = -8.0089)
iso <- ox_isochrone(g, centre, cutoffs = c(60, 120), weight = "travel_time")
iso[c("cutoff", "n_nodes")]
```

```{r}
plot(g, col = "grey85", lwd = 0.6)
plot(sf::st_geometry(iso), add = TRUE, border = NA,
     col = grDevices::adjustcolor(c("#0d3b66", "#2a9d8f"), 0.4))
```

## Many-to-many distances

For accessibility work you often need a full origin–destination matrix in one
call (see the [Accessibility](accessibility.html) article):

```{r}
hubs <- ox_nearest_nodes(g,
  x = c(-34.8553, -34.8505, -34.852),
  y = c(-8.0089, -8.0125, -8.006))
round(ox_distance_matrix(g, hubs, hubs, weight = "travel_time"))
```

## Blending new stops into the network

Routing starts and ends at nodes, but real origins and destinations rarely
sit on one — `ox_nearest_nodes()` above quietly moved them to the closest
intersection. `ox_blend()` does better: it snaps each point onto its nearest
*edge* and splits the edge there (in both directions of a two-way street),
turning the exact location into a routable node — the `osmnxr` counterpart of
`sfnetworks::st_network_blend()`, computed in the Rust core:

```{r}
stops <- sf::st_sfc(
  sf::st_point(c(-34.8540, -8.0095)),
  sf::st_point(c(-34.8512, -8.0118)),
  crs = sf::st_crs(g$nodes)
)
gb <- ox_blend(g, stops)
gb$meta$blend # which node each stop became, and how far it was snapped

ox_route_shortest(gb, gb$meta$blend$node[1], gb$meta$blend$node[2],
                  weight = "travel_time")
```

`ox_blend()` also accepts a whole second `osm_graph` (say, a metro layer over
a street network): every node of the second graph is snapped into the first,
the two graphs are stacked with `ox_union()`, and *connector* edges are added
between each snapped pair — producing one routable multimodal graph. See
`?ox_blend` for the details.

## References

Boeing, G. (2025). Modeling and analyzing urban networks and amenities with
OSMnx. *Geographical Analysis*.
